# Lessons from the Antiretroviral Therapy Case Study {#sec-case-study-synthesis}

*Estimated reading time: 10 minutes*









Throughout this handbook we have leaned on one dataset, the longitudinal HIV antiretroviral therapy cohort [@vanderwal2011ipw], to illustrate every major concept, from defining a causal question to diagnosing how an estimator behaves [@petersen2014causal; @dang2023causal; @hernan2025whatif]. This closing section gathers the lessons and follows the path from naive methods to principled causal estimation. For the full data description, including the variable dictionary and target trial protocol, see the [Running Case Study](00-case-study.qmd).

## What a naive analysis might have done

Without the roadmap, a researcher would likely fit a Cox or pooled logistic regression, adjust for time-varying CD4 because it is a confounder, and report the hazard ratio as the effect of highly active antiretroviral therapy (HAART). Two of those moves are the traps we developed earlier in the book. Adjusting for CD4 blocks part of the treatment effect, since CD4 is itself affected by prior treatment (@sec-longitudinal-confounding), and the hazard ratio answers a different question than the one a clinician asks (@sec-regression-vs-causal). As the running case study shows, the upshot can make an effective treatment look harmful.

## How the Causal Roadmap clarified the question

Running the seven steps of @sec-roadmap on this cohort fixed each of those problems before any model was fit. A target trial protocol set the question: the effect on mortality of initiating HAART at seroconversion versus not. A directed acyclic graph (DAG) made the dual role of CD4 explicit, a confounder of future treatment and a mediator of past treatment. The estimand was the marginal risk difference, not a hazard ratio. And the identification assumptions (exchangeability, consistency, positivity) were stated alongside where they might fail, namely unmeasured adherence and clinical staging. Only then were g-computation [@robins1986gformula], IPTW (inverse probability of treatment weighting), and TMLE (targeted maximum likelihood estimation) [@vanderLaan2006tmle] applied and compared, using Super Learner [@vanderLaan2007superlearner] for flexible nuisance estimation.

## Why time-dependent confounding required longitudinal methods

The central lesson of this case study is that **standard regression cannot handle treatment-confounder feedback**. When a time-varying confounder (`cd4.sqrt`) is both a consequence of prior treatment (`haartind`) and a cause of future treatment, the analyst faces an impossible choice in a regression framework:

- **Do not adjust for time-varying CD4:** leaves confounding of future treatment unaddressed.
- **Adjust for time-varying CD4:** blocks part of the treatment effect, and can introduce collider bias when CD4 shares an unmeasured common cause with the outcome.

Neither option produces a consistent estimate of the causal effect, as @sec-longitudinal-confounding demonstrates concretely. The g-methods (g-computation, IPTW with marginal structural models [@robins2000msm], longitudinal TMLE) escape the dilemma by separating the treatment mechanism from the outcome mechanism, modeling one or both explicitly, then reweighting (IPTW) or standardizing (g-computation) rather than naively conditioning; TMLE combines both. @sec-illustrated-ltmle walked through the mechanics of longitudinal TMLE step by step: backwards sequential regression conditions on `cd4.sqrt` where it confounds future treatment and integrates it out where it mediates past treatment. This is not a minor technical improvement. It changes what can be estimated at all.

## What the example illustrates about real-world evidence analyses

The HIV/HAART example is not unique. Treatment-confounder feedback arises whenever:

- Treatment decisions respond to time-varying patient status (lab values, symptoms, disease progression)
- Those same patient characteristics are also affected by prior treatment
- The outcome of interest occurs at the end of a follow-up period during which both treatment and confounders evolve

The pattern is common in chronic disease epidemiology, pharmacoepidemiology, and comparative effectiveness research. A few examples:

- Insulin dose adjustments based on HbA1c in diabetes
- Immunosuppressant dosing based on kidney function in transplant recipients
- Chemotherapy regimen changes based on tumor markers in oncology
- Blood pressure medication titration based on BP readings

In every one of these settings, estimating causal effects correctly calls for the methods covered in this handbook rather than standard regression. The Causal Roadmap supplies the structure, and the estimation methods (g-computation, IPTW, TMLE, longitudinal TMLE) supply the tools.

## Summary

@tbl-approach-comparison lays out how each approach handles confounding, treatment-confounder feedback, marginal effects, and valid inference.




::: {#tbl-approach-comparison .cell layout-align="center" tbl-cap='Comparison of approaches for the HAART case study'}

```{.r .cell-code  code-fold="true"}
source("_data/load-haart-cohort.R")

# Final summary table of approaches and their limitations
tibble::tribble(
  ~Approach, ~`Handles confounding`, ~`Handles feedback`, ~`Marginal effect`, ~`Valid inference`,
  "Crude comparison",          "No",  "No",  "Yes", "No",
  "Baseline regression",       "Partially", "No", "No (conditional)", "Yes (if correct)",
  "Time-varying regression",   "Partially", "No (biased)", "No (conditional)", "Yes (if correct)",
  "G-computation",             "Yes", "Yes (longitudinal)", "Yes", "Bootstrap only",
  "IPTW / MSM",                "Yes", "Yes", "Yes", "Sandwich SE",
  "TMLE",                      "Yes", "Yes (longitudinal)", "Yes", "Influence curve"
) |>
  knitr::kable()
```

::: {.cell-output-display}


|Approach                |Handles confounding |Handles feedback   |Marginal effect  |Valid inference  |
|:-----------------------|:-------------------|:------------------|:----------------|:----------------|
|Crude comparison        |No                  |No                 |Yes              |No               |
|Baseline regression     |Partially           |No                 |No (conditional) |Yes (if correct) |
|Time-varying regression |Partially           |No (biased)        |No (conditional) |Yes (if correct) |
|G-computation           |Yes                 |Yes (longitudinal) |Yes              |Bootstrap only   |
|IPTW / MSM              |Yes                 |Yes                |Yes              |Sandwich SE      |
|TMLE                    |Yes                 |Yes (longitudinal) |Yes              |Influence curve  |


:::
:::




Even after longitudinal methods, the results still rest on untestable identification assumptions. @sec-advanced-diagnostics showed how to probe that dependence with E-values [@vanderweele2017evalue], quantitative bias analysis, and truncation sensitivity. For the HAART cohort, unmeasured adherence is the most plausible threat: patients who adhere to treatment tend to be healthier, which can inflate the apparent benefit. A sensitivity analysis tells us how strong such confounding would have to be to explain away the estimated effect.

The move from naive regression to longitudinal TMLE is not sophistication for its own sake. Each step solves a concrete problem the previous approach could not. The antiretroviral therapy case study makes both the problems and their solutions tangible.
